Elders who fought for the Kauravas out of duty to Hastinapura despite sympathy for the Pandavas: Bhishma, Drona and Kripa.
Karna, Shalya and Kritavarma joined Duryodhana from friendship, obligation and alliance respectively; Yuyutsu, a son of Dhritarashtra, defected to the Pandavas.

Bhishma — Devavrata, grandsire of the Ku: Bhishma, born Devavrata, was the eighth son of King Shantanu and the river goddess Ganga, and the only one she did not drown; he was an incarnation of one of the eight Vasus cursed by the sage Vasishtha, the one the Adi Parva names Dyaus (Dyu), who stole Vasishtha's cow at his wife's urging; some later lists and retellings call this Vasu Prabhasa.
Devavrata was taught by Vasishtha, Brihaspati, Shukra and Parashurama, and was made crown prince of Hastinapura.
To let his father marry Satyavati, Devavrata renounced the throne and vowed lifelong celibacy so no child of his could claim it; the gods named him Bhishma ('the terrible one') for this vow.
Shantanu granted Bhishma the boon of choosing the time of his own death (icchamrityu).
Bhishma abducted the three princesses of Kashi, Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, from their svayamvara as brides for his half-brother Vichitravirya.
When Bhishma refused to marry Amba, his teacher Parashurama fought him on her behalf; the Udyoga Parva says the duel lasted twenty-three days without a victor.
Bhishma served as regent and protector of the Kuru throne for generations, under Chitrangada, Vichitravirya, Pandu, Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana; he saw his vow as binding him to Hastinapura.
Bhishma failed to answer Draupadi's question in the dice hall, saying the course of dharma was subtle, a silence that critics of the epic and its characters still debate.
Bhishma was Kaurava supreme commander for the first ten days of the war, though he declared he would not kill the Pandavas themselves.
On the night of day 9 Bhishma told the Pandavas he would not fight Shikhandi; on day 10 Arjuna, shooting from behind Shikhandi, brought him down onto a bed of arrows.
Lying on the bed of arrows, Bhishma asked for water, and Arjuna shot an arrow into the earth to bring up a spring.
Bhishma waited for the sun's northward course (uttarayana) to die; in the Anushasana Parva he says he has lain fifty-eight nights on the arrows.

From the bed of arrows Bhishma taught Yudhishthira on kingship, conduct in crisis and liberation (Shanti Parva) and on duty and gifts (Anushasana Parva), where the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu, is placed in his mouth.
Bhishma's death and his mother Ganga's lament close the Anushasana Parva.
Drona — Dronacharya, teacher of the Kuru: Drona was the son of the sage Bharadvaja, born, as his name ('vessel') indicates, from his father's seed collected in a pot; the Adi Parva makes him a portion of Brihaspati.
Drona married Kripi, sister of Kripa, and their son was Ashwatthama.
Drona received weapons and the knowledge to use them from Parashurama, who was giving away all his possessions.
Poor and scorned by his boyhood friend King Drupada, Drona came to Hastinapura, where he retrieved the princes' ball from a well with blades of grass and was appointed their teacher by Bhishma.
As teacher's fee Drona demanded that his pupils capture Drupada; Arjuna did so, and Drona kept northern Panchala.
Drona demanded the right thumb of the Nishada archer Ekalavya, who had learned before a clay image of him, to keep his promise that Arjuna would be the greatest archer.
Drona tested his pupils by asking what they saw when aiming at a wooden bird; only Arjuna said he saw only the bird's eye.
Drona fought for the Kauravas and was supreme commander from day 11 to day 15, vowing to capture Yudhishthira alive.
On day 13 Drona's chakravyuha formation trapped Abhimanyu, and on day 15 Drona killed his old rival Drupada and King Virata.
On day 15 Bhima killed an elephant named Ashvatthama; Yudhishthira confirmed to Drona that 'Ashvatthama' was dead, adding indistinctly that it was an elephant, and Drona laid down his arms.
Seated in yogic meditation, Drona was beheaded by Dhrishtadyumna; the Drona Parva says his spirit had already left his body for heaven.

Drona is often criticised, in the epic and in modern readings, for his treatment of Ekalavya and for his partiality to Arjuna and his own son; the popular scene of Drona refusing to teach Karna because of his birth comes from later retellings, since in the epic Karna is listed among Drona's pupils.
Kripa — Kripacharya, first teacher of th: Kripa (Kripacharya) and his twin sister Kripi were born to the sage Sharadvan Gautama when his seed fell on a clump of reeds at the sight of the apsara Janapadi.
King Shantanu found the abandoned twins and raised them out of compassion (kripa), which gave them their names.
Kripa was the first teacher of arms to the Kuru princes before Drona arrived; his sister Kripi married Drona.
Kripa fought for the Kauravas throughout the war and repeatedly counselled Duryodhana to make peace.
Kripa was one of the three Kaurava survivors, with Ashwatthama and Kritavarma, and took part in the night raid by guarding the camp's gates.
After the war Kripa was appointed teacher of Parikshit; later tradition counts him among the seven chiranjivis (long-lived immortals).
Vidura — wise minister, son of Vyasa: Vidura was the son of Vyasa by a maidservant whom Ambika sent in her place for the niyoga; he was the half-brother of Dhritarashtra and Pandu.
Vidura was an incarnation of Dharma (Yama), cursed by the sage Animandavya to be born of a shudra mother for punishing him unjustly.
Because of his birth Vidura could not be king; he served as chief counsellor of Hastinapura and was famed for his wisdom and honesty.
Vidura warned the Pandavas of the lac house in a coded speech and sent a miner to dig their escape tunnel.
Vidura opposed the dice game, was abused by Duryodhana, and briefly left Hastinapura to visit the Pandavas in exile before Dhritarashtra recalled him.
Vidura's night-time counsel to the sleepless Dhritarashtra in the Udyoga Parva is known as the Vidura Niti.
During his peace mission Krishna refused Duryodhana's hospitality and stayed in Vidura's house, where Kunti was living.
Vidura did not fight in the war; some retellings say he broke his bow in protest, a detail that is not well attested in the Critical Edition.
Vidura retired to the forest with Dhritarashtra; when Yudhishthira found him, emaciated, Vidura passed his life force into Yudhishthira's body through yoga and died (Ashramavasika Parva).
Vyasa — Krishna Dvaipayana, author and g: Vyasa, called Krishna Dvaipayana ('the dark one born on an island'), was the son of the sage Parashara and Satyavati, born on an island in the Yamuna before her marriage to Shantanu.
Tradition credits Vyasa with arranging the Vedas, hence the title Vedavyasa, and with composing the Mahabharata; he is also a character in the story.
At his mother's request Vyasa fathered Dhritarashtra (with Ambika), Pandu (with Ambalika) and Vidura (with a maidservant) by niyoga, so he is the biological grandfather of both Kauravas and Pandavas.
Vyasa taught the epic to his pupil Vaishampayana, who recited it at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice; his son was the sage Shuka.

The Adi Parva says Vyasa composed a Bharata of 24,000 verses without the subsidiary tales, and speaks of a larger work; it also mentions 8,800 verses that only Vyasa, Shuka and perhaps Sanjaya understand.
The story that Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as Vyasa dictated it is a later addition; the Critical Edition places it outside the main text.
Vyasa intervenes repeatedly: dividing Gandhari's flesh into 101 pots, explaining Draupadi's marriage, giving Sanjaya divine sight, stopping the Brahmashira duel and urging Yudhishthira to rule.
In the Ashramavasika Parva Vyasa summoned the dead warriors from the Ganga for one night so their families could see them again.
After Krishna's death Vyasa told the grieving Arjuna that his time had passed, prompting the Pandavas' final journey.
Later tradition counts Vyasa among the seven chiranjivis (long-lived immortals).
Sanjaya — charioteer and narrator of the: Sanjaya, son of Gavalgana, was charioteer (suta) and counsellor to King Dhritarashtra.
Before the war Sanjaya went to the Pandavas as Dhritarashtra's envoy and brought back their message.
Vyasa gave Sanjaya divine sight so that he could see and narrate the whole war to Dhritarashtra, including the thoughts of the combatants.
Sanjaya narrates the Bhagavad Gita to Dhritarashtra in the Bhishma Parva, beginning with Dhritarashtra's question about what his sons and Pandu's sons did at Kurukshetra.
Sanjaya speaks frankly to Dhritarashtra, often telling him his own failings caused the disaster.
On day 18 Sanjaya was captured on the battlefield and spared, according to the Shalya Parva, after Vyasa's intervention.
Sanjaya accompanied Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti to the forest, survived the forest fire that killed them and went to the Himalaya.
Satyavati — fisher queen, matriarch of t: The Adi Parva says Satyavati was born from a fish (a cursed apsara) that swallowed the seed of King Uparichara Vasu, and was raised by the chief of the fisherfolk (Dasharaja).
Satyavati was called Matsyagandha for her fishy smell until the sage Parashara gave her a fragrance carried for a yojana (Yojanagandha); their son was Vyasa.
Satyavati's father agreed to her marriage with King Shantanu only if her sons would inherit, which led to Bhishma's vow.
Satyavati's sons by Shantanu were Chitrangada, killed by a gandharva of the same name, and Vichitravirya, who died childless of a wasting illness.
To save the dynasty Satyavati asked Bhishma to father heirs (he refused, citing his vow) and then summoned her first son Vyasa for niyoga with Vichitravirya's widows.
After Pandu's death, on Vyasa's advice, Satyavati withdrew to the forest with Ambika and Ambalika and died there.
Satyavati's descendants: sons 3 (Vyasa, Chitrangada, Vichitravirya) | grandsons by niyoga 3 (Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura)
Shantanu — Kuru king, father of Bhishma: Shantanu was a Kuru king of Hastinapura, son of King Pratipa; the Adi Parva makes him a rebirth of King Mahabhisha.
The Adi Parva says Shantanu's touch made the old young again, which it uses to explain his name.
Shantanu married Ganga on condition that he never question her; she drowned seven newborn sons, and when he protested at the eighth she left, revealing the curse of the Vasus.
Ganga later returned his grown son Devavrata (Bhishma) to Shantanu, trained in scripture and arms.
Shantanu fell in love with Satyavati; Devavrata's vow of celibacy and renunciation made the marriage possible.
Shantanu gave Bhishma the boon that he would die only when he chose.
Shantanu's sons: by Ganga 8 (7 drowned, Devavrata survived) | by Satyavati 2 (Chitrangada, Vichitravirya)
Shantanu also found and raised the twins Kripa and Kripi.
Ganga — river goddess, mother of Bhishma: Ganga, goddess of the river Ganges, agreed to become the mother of the eight Vasus, who had been cursed by Vasishtha to be born as humans for stealing his wish-granting cow Nandini.
Ganga married Shantanu on condition that he never question her actions.
Ganga drowned seven of their sons at birth to free those Vasus at once; the eighth, the Vasu who had actually stolen the cow, had to live a long life on earth without offspring.
When Shantanu objected at the eighth birth, Ganga left him, taking the child, and later returned him as the accomplished Devavrata.
Ganga appears at the end of the Anushasana Parva mourning Bhishma's death, and Krishna and Vyasa console her.
Ganga as a sacred river runs through the epic, where the dead are honoured with water offerings and Vyasa calls up the slain warriors from its waters.
Amba — princess of Kashi, Bhishma's neme: Amba was the eldest of the three princesses of Kashi abducted by Bhishma from their svayamvara for Vichitravirya; her sisters were Ambika and Ambalika.
Amba told Bhishma she had chosen King Shalva of Saubha; Bhishma let her go, but Shalva rejected her because another man had carried her off.
Amba demanded that Bhishma marry her; bound by his vow, he refused.
Amba sought help from Parashurama, who fought Bhishma for twenty-three days without winning, and then turned to austerities.
Skanda (Kartikeya) gave Amba a garland of unfading lotuses, promising that its wearer would kill Bhishma; Drupada would not wear it, and it hung on his gate.
Shiva granted Amba that she would kill Bhishma in her next birth; she entered a fire and was reborn as Drupada's child Shikhandini, later Shikhandi.
Amba's story is told mainly in the Udyoga Parva (the Ambopakhyana), as Bhishma's own explanation for refusing to fight Shikhandi.
Ekalavya — the Nishada archer: Ekalavya was a Nishada (a forest people), son of the Nishada chief Hiranyadhanus.
Drona refused to accept Ekalavya as a pupil; Ekalavya made a clay image of Drona in the forest and practised archery before it until he became a superb archer.
When the Pandavas' dog barked at him, Ekalavya silenced it with seven arrows in its mouth without injuring it, which revealed his skill to the princes.
Drona, having promised Arjuna that no one would surpass him, asked Ekalavya for his right thumb as teacher's fee, and Ekalavya cut it off without hesitation.
After losing his thumb Ekalavya shot with his fingers and was less swift than before (Adi Parva).
Later passages and texts associate Ekalavya with Jarasandha and connect his death with Krishna; these references are brief and vary between versions.
Ekalavya's story is widely read today as a story of caste and exclusion, and as a critique of Drona.
Pandu — the pale king, father of the Pan: Pandu was the son of Vichitravirya's widow Ambalika by Vyasa through niyoga; the Adi Parva says he was born pale because Ambalika turned pale with fear at the sight of the sage, and his name means 'the pale one'.
Because Dhritarashtra was blind, Pandu was crowned king of Hastinapura, and the Adi Parva describes his campaigns of conquest that enlarged the Kuru realm.
Pandu married Kunti, who chose him at her svayamvara, and Madri of Madra, obtained by Bhishma for a bride-price.
While hunting, Pandu shot the sage Kindama, who was mating with his wife in the form of a deer; the dying sage cursed Pandu to die if he ever approached a wife in love.
Pandu renounced the throne and lived as an ascetic in the forest (the Adi Parva mentions the Shatashringa mountain) with Kunti and Madri, leaving Dhritarashtra to govern.
Desperate for heirs, Pandu urged Kunti to bear sons by others; she revealed Durvasa's mantra, and the five Pandavas were born to Kunti and Madri through the gods.
Pandu died in the forest when he embraced Madri in springtime, and Madri followed him onto his funeral pyre; the sages then brought Kunti and the five boys to Hastinapura.
Pandu is thus the legal father of the five Pandavas but the biological father of none of them, which shapes the later dispute over who is the rightful heir to the Kuru throne.
Partial incarnations of the main charact: The Adi Parva's list of partial incarnations (amshavatarana) gives a divine or demonic origin for many characters; these attributions vary somewhat between versions.
Divine origins of elders: Bhishma a Vasu | Drona Brihaspati | Ashwatthama Shiva, Yama, Kama and Krodha | Vidura Dharma | Kripa one of the Rudras
Divine origins on the Kaurava side: Duryodhana Kali | Shakuni Dvapara | Karna Surya | Gandhari Mati
Divine origins on the Pandava side: Krishna Narayana | Balarama the serpent Shesha | Draupadi Shri | Dhrishtadyumna Agni | Abhimanyu Varchas son of Soma | Kunti Siddhi | Madri Dhriti
The Adi Parva also places Satyaki, Kritavarma, Drupada and Virata among warriors born from the Maruts (storm gods).
The Pandavas are sons of the gods Dharma, Vayu, Indra and the Ashvins, and the same Adi Parva list also calls them portions of those gods; a separate Adi Parva story makes them five former Indras.
Teachers, pupils and lineages of learnin: Teachers and their pupils: Parashurama Bhishma, Drona, Karna | Drona Pandavas, Kauravas, Karna, Dhrishtadyumna | Kripa Kuru princes, later Parikshit | Balarama Duryodhana and Bhima (mace) | Arjuna Satyaki and Abhimanyu

Parashurama taught three great warriors of the epic: Drona received his weapons as a gift, Bhishma later fought him for 23 days over Amba, and Karna was cursed to forget the Brahmastra when his deception was discovered.
Vyasa's narrative lineage: Vyasa taught Vaishampayana, who recited to Janamejaya; Ugrashravas (Sauti) heard it there and retold it to the sages at Naimisha forest.
Ekalavya learned from a clay image of Drona, without Drona's consent.
Neutral, non-combatant and elder figures: Elders who fought for the Kauravas: Bhishma | Drona | Kripa | Shalya
Elders and others who did not fight: Vidura | Dhritarashtra | Gandhari | Kunti | Vyasa | Sanjaya (narrator) | Balarama (went on pilgrimage)

Generations of the Kuru story (oldest first): Shantanu, Ganga, Satyavati | Bhishma, Vyasa, Chitrangada, Vichitravirya | Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura | Kauravas, Pandavas, Karna | Abhimanyu, Upapandavas, Ghatotkacha | Parikshit | Janamejaya

Fates of the elders: Bhishma died on the bed of arrows after the war | Drona killed on day 15 | Kripa survived | Vidura died in the forest | Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti died in a forest fire | Sanjaya went to the Himalaya | Vyasa lived on
Bhishma, Kripa and Vyasa span the whole story, from Shantanu's reign to after the war; Vidura spans from the generation after Shantanu to the elders' last years in the forest.

Krishna — birth, family and early life: Krishna was the son of the Yadava (Vrishni) prince Vasudeva and Devaki, sister of the tyrant Kamsa of Mathura; to escape Kamsa he was raised by the cowherd Nanda and his wife Yashoda in Gokula (Vraja).

Krishna's childhood and youth (the cowherd life, the slaying of demons, his love with the gopis and his killing of Kamsa) are told mainly in the Harivamsha (the Mahabharata's appendix) and the Puranas, especially the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas; the Mahabharata itself mostly alludes to them, as in Shishupala's insults in the Sabha Parva.
Krishna was a cousin of the Pandavas: his father Vasudeva was the brother of Kunti (Pritha), so Kunti was Krishna's paternal aunt.
Krishna's family: father Vasudeva | mother Devaki | foster father Nanda | foster mother Yashoda | elder brother Balarama | sister Subhadra | maternal uncle Kamsa | paternal aunt Kunti
Krishna's names and epithets include Vasudeva, Keshava, Madhava, Govinda, Hrishikesha, Janardana, Madhusudana, Achyuta and Partha-sarathi (Arjuna's charioteer).
The epic identifies Krishna with Narayana (Vishnu) and Arjuna with Nara, the paired ancient sages, a link stated repeatedly in the Mahabharata.

After killing Kamsa, Krishna led the Yadavas from Mathura to Dwaraka on the western sea to escape the repeated attacks of Jarasandha of Magadha, Kamsa's father-in-law (Sabha Parva; the Puranas count the attacks as seventeen or eighteen).
Krishna — weapons, conch, chariot and at: Krishna's weapons: discus Sudarshana | mace Kaumodaki | bow Sharnga | sword Nandaka; his conch is Panchajanya.
Agni gave Krishna the discus and the mace Kaumodaki at the burning of the Khandava forest, when he gave Arjuna the Gandiva bow (Adi Parva).
Krishna's conch Panchajanya is named in the Bhagavad Gita (1.15); the Puranas say it came from the sea demon Panchajana.
Krishna's own chariot horses are named Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Balahaka, and his charioteer is Daruka.
Krishna's banner bears Garuda, the eagle mount of Vishnu.
Krishna is described as dark-skinned, dressed in yellow garments, and wearing the Kaustubha jewel and the Shrivatsa mark in Vaishnava descriptions.
Krishna and the Pandavas — friendship, K: Krishna first meets the Pandavas at Draupadi's svayamvara, where he recognises them in their brahmin disguise.
Krishna and Arjuna are close friends and cousins; Krishna approved Arjuna's elopement with his sister Subhadra and persuaded Balarama to accept it.
Krishna and Arjuna burned the Khandava forest together for the fire god Agni, fighting off Indra, and spared Maya, who built the Pandavas' assembly hall.

Krishna advised Yudhishthira that Jarasandha had to be removed before the Rajasuya; disguised as brahmins, Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna went to Magadha, where Bhima killed Jarasandha in a wrestling duel and the imprisoned kings were freed.

At the Rajasuya, Krishna received the first honour on Bhishma's advice; Shishupala of Chedi protested and insulted him, and Krishna killed Shishupala with his discus after exhausting the hundred offences he had promised Shishupala's mother to forgive.
Krishna was absent from the dice game; in the Vana Parva he explains that he was away fighting King Shalva of Saubha, who had attacked Dwaraka.
During the exile Krishna visited the Pandavas in the forest and promised Draupadi that her humiliation would be avenged.
Popular retellings make Krishna the rescuer of Draupadi's honour in the dice hall; the Critical Edition keeps the miracle of the endless garment but places her prayer to Krishna in an appendix.

The story of Krishna saving the exiled Pandavas from the hungry sage Durvasa and his disciples by eating a last morsel left in Draupadi's vessel belongs to the vulgate and popular tradition; it is not part of the Critical Edition's constituted text.
Krishna's peace embassy and the road to: Before the war Arjuna and Duryodhana both went to Dwaraka for Krishna's help; Krishna, waking to see Arjuna first, let him choose between Krishna alone, unarmed and not fighting, and Krishna's army.

Arjuna chose Krishna himself; Duryodhana gladly took Krishna's Narayana troops, which the Udyoga Parva describes as a huge force of cowherd warriors and which popular accounts often call one akshauhini.

Krishna went to Hastinapura as the Pandavas' envoy, stayed with Vidura and pleaded for peace in the Kuru assembly; the Pandavas' request was reduced to five villages (the names vary between passages and versions).
When Duryodhana plotted to seize him, Krishna revealed his cosmic form (vishvarupa) in the Kuru court (Udyoga Parva).

After the failed embassy Krishna met Karna alone, revealed that Karna was Kunti's eldest son and offered him the throne and Draupadi if he joined the Pandavas; Karna refused out of loyalty to Duryodhana.
Debate continues over whether Krishna sincerely sought peace or knew the war to be inevitable; the epic gives him speeches pointing both ways.
Krishna in the Kurukshetra war — chariot: Krishna served as Arjuna's charioteer throughout the war and vowed not to take up weapons.
Before the first day's battle Krishna taught Arjuna the Bhagavad Gita (Bhishma Parva), 700 verses in 18 chapters in the received text, and revealed his universal form.

On day 3 and again on day 9 Krishna, angered by Arjuna's mild fighting against Bhishma, leapt from the chariot to attack Bhishma himself, with his discus in some passages and a whip in others; popular retellings show him raising a chariot wheel. Arjuna held him back.
Krishna saved Arjuna from Bhagadatta's Vaishnava weapon on day 12 by taking it on his own chest, where it became a garland.
When Ashwatthama released the Narayanastra on day 15, Krishna saved the Pandava army by telling the warriors to lay down their arms.

Krishna advised or approved most of the stratagems by which the Kaurava champions fell: Shikhandi before Bhishma, the false report of Ashwatthama's death to Drona, the attack on Karna while his wheel was stuck, and Bhima's blow to Duryodhana's thigh.
Krishna also intervened on the day of Jayadratha's death and rejoiced at Ghatotkacha's death because it used up Karna's Vasavi spear.
When the heavens honoured the fallen Duryodhana, Krishna told the Pandavas that the Kaurava heroes could not have been killed by fair means, and defended the stratagems as necessary.
After the night massacre Krishna cursed Ashwatthama to wander for three thousand years and revived Uttaraa's stillborn son Parikshit.
Krishna after the war — teachings, curse: After the war Krishna urged the grieving Yudhishthira to rule and took him to hear Bhishma's teachings on the bed of arrows.

Gandhari cursed Krishna in the Stri Parva: since he had allowed the Kurus to destroy one another, his own clan would perish by fratricide in thirty-six years, and he would die alone; Krishna accepted the curse.
In the Ashvamedhika Parva Krishna retells his teaching to Arjuna, who says he has forgotten the Gita; this second teaching is called the Anugita.
Krishna's death (Mausala Parva): after the Yadavas destroyed themselves, he sat in meditation in the forest and was struck in the foot by the arrow of a hunter named Jara, who took him for a deer.
Krishna forgave Jara and departed to heaven; Arjuna arrived in Dwaraka to find Krishna gone and his father Vasudeva dying.
Traditional Indian reckoning dates the start of the Kali age to Krishna's departure (conventionally 3102 BCE); this is a traditional calculation, not a historically established date.
The Bhagavata Purana says Krishna lived about 125 years; the Mahabharata gives no explicit age.
Krishna's wives, sons and descendants: Krishna's chief wife is Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha, whom he carried off with her consent despite her brother Rukmi (a story told mainly in the Harivamsha and Puranas, and only alluded to in the Mahabharata); Satyabhama and Jambavati are among his other prominent wives.
The Puranas list eight principal wives (ashtabharya): Rukmini, Satyabhama, Jambavati, Kalindi, Mitravinda, Nagnajiti (Satya), Bhadra and Lakshmana; the eight vary slightly between texts.
The Mahabharata mentions sixteen thousand wives of Krishna; the Bhagavata Purana gives 16,100 women rescued from the demon Naraka in addition to the eight chief wives.
Krishna's wives (traditional counts): principal 8 | others 16,000 (Mahabharata) or 16,100 (Bhagavata Purana)
Krishna's best-known sons are Pradyumna (by Rukmini), Samba (by Jambavati) and Charudeshna; his grandson Aniruddha was Pradyumna's son.

The Bhagavata Purana and related later texts say Samba carried off and married Lakshmanaa, daughter of Duryodhana, making Krishna and Duryodhana relatives by marriage; the Mahabharata itself does not tell this story.
Krishna's great-grandson Vajra, son of Aniruddha, survived the Yadava destruction and was installed by Arjuna as ruler at Indraprastha (Mausala Parva).
In the Vana Parva Satyabhama asks Draupadi how she keeps her five husbands devoted, and Draupadi describes her conduct and service.
Balarama — Krishna's elder brother: Balarama (Baladeva, Sankarshana) was Krishna's elder brother, son of Vasudeva and Rohini; the Harivamsha and Puranas say he was transferred as an embryo from Devaki's womb to Rohini's.
Balarama carries the plough (hala), giving him the name Halayudha, and the pestle-club (musala); he is famed for his strength and fair complexion, and his wife was Revati.
The Adi Parva makes Balarama a partial incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha.
Balarama taught mace combat to both Duryodhana and Bhima and was fond of Duryodhana.
Balarama was angry when Arjuna carried off Subhadra, until Krishna persuaded him to accept the marriage.
Balarama refused to fight for either side and went on a pilgrimage along the Sarasvati river during the war; the Shalya Parva says he was away forty-two days.

Balarama returned in time to watch the mace duel between Bhima and Duryodhana; enraged at Bhima's blow below the navel, he raised his plough to attack Bhima, was calmed by Krishna and left for Dwaraka, declaring that Duryodhana would reach heaven.
At the end of the Yadavas, Balarama sat in yogic meditation by the sea and a great white serpent left his mouth and entered the ocean (Mausala Parva).
Balarama is worshipped as Balabhadra with Jagannatha and Subhadra at Puri, and in some traditions he replaces the Buddha in the list of Vishnu's ten avatars.
Satyaki (Yuyudhana) — Yadava champion of: Satyaki, also called Yuyudhana, was a Yadava warrior of the Shini (Shaineya) clan, grandson of Shini and son of Satyaka.
Satyaki learned archery from Arjuna and was devoted to both Arjuna and Krishna.
Satyaki accompanied Krishna on the peace embassy to Hastinapura and warned him of Duryodhana's plot to seize him.
Satyaki brought one akshauhini to the Pandavas and was one of the seven Pandava commanders.
On day 14 Satyaki, sent by Yudhishthira to help Arjuna, broke through the Kaurava formations.
On day 14 Satyaki was overpowered by Bhurishravas; Arjuna cut off Bhurishravas's arm, and when Bhurishravas sat down to fast to death, Satyaki beheaded him, an act condemned by many on both sides.
The feud between Satyaki's Shini clan and Bhurishravas's family went back to Shini's defeat of Somadatta when winning Devaki as a bride for Vasudeva.
Satyaki survived the war, one of the seven Pandava-side survivors.
Satyaki died in the drunken Yadava brawl at Prabhasa, killed by the Bhojas and Andhakas after he had beheaded Kritavarma.
Kritavarma — Yadava warrior on the Kaura: Kritavarma was a Yadava of the Bhoja (Andhaka) branch, son of Hridika.
Kritavarma brought one akshauhini to Duryodhana and fought for the Kauravas throughout the war, the most prominent Yadava on that side.
Kritavarma was one of the three Kaurava survivors with Ashwatthama and Kripa.
In the night raid Kritavarma and Kripa guarded the gates of the Pandava camp, cut down those who fled and set the camp on fire.

At Prabhasa, thirty-six years after the war, the drunken Satyaki mocked Kritavarma for the night massacre; Kritavarma taunted Satyaki over Bhurishravas, and Satyaki beheaded him, starting the brawl that destroyed the Yadavas.
The Puranas involve Kritavarma in the quarrel over the Syamantaka jewel and the killing of its owner Satrajit; that story belongs to the Puranic tradition, not the Mahabharata's main narrative.
The Yadava clan — branches, Dwaraka and: The Yadavas descend from Yadu, eldest son of King Yayati; the Adi Parva says Yayati cursed Yadu's line not to hold royal sovereignty after Yadu refused to give his father his youth.
The Yadava branches include the Vrishnis (Krishna's own line), Andhakas, Bhojas, Kukuras, Shainyas (Shini's line), Dasharhas and Satvatas, often grouped as the Vrishni-Andhaka confederacy.
The Yadavas were governed as a clan assembly; King Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, was restored as their nominal king after Krishna killed Kamsa.

Dwaraka, the Yadava capital, is described as a strongly fortified city on the western sea (some descriptions make it island-like, surrounded by water); it is traditionally identified with Dwarka in Gujarat, and claims about submerged ruins offshore are debated.
The Yadavas were split by the war: allegiances: Krishna Pandavas (unarmed) | Satyaki Pandavas | Chekitana Pandavas | Kritavarma Kauravas | Narayana troops Kauravas | Balarama neutral
Yadava festivals at Mount Raivataka near Dwaraka were the setting of Arjuna's elopement with Subhadra.
Leading Yadava figures include Ugrasena, Vasudeva, Akrura, Balarama, Krishna, Satyaki, Kritavarma, Uddhava, Pradyumna, Samba and Aniruddha.
Destruction of the Yadavas (Mausala Parv: In the thirty-sixth year after the war, fulfilling Gandhari's curse, the Yadavas destroyed themselves (Mausala Parva).

Some young Yadavas dressed Krishna's son Samba as a pregnant woman and asked the sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada what she would bear; the sages cursed them that Samba would bear an iron pestle (musala) that would destroy the clan.
Samba gave birth to an iron pestle; King Ugrasena had it ground to powder and thrown into the sea, and liquor was banned in Dwaraka, but omens multiplied.
The powdered iron washed ashore and grew into eraka reeds.

The Yadavas went on a pilgrimage to Prabhasa by the sea, drank heavily, and quarrelled; Satyaki killed Kritavarma, Satyaki and Pradyumna were killed, and the Yadavas slaughtered one another with eraka reeds that turned into iron clubs in their hands.
Krishna himself joined the killing in fury, then left; Balarama departed in yoga, and Krishna was killed by the hunter Jara's arrow.
Arjuna came to Dwaraka, performed the rites for Vasudeva and led the surviving women, children and elders away; the sea then swallowed Dwaraka.
On the way, in the land of the five rivers (Panchanada), Abhira herdsmen attacked the convoy; Arjuna could barely string Gandiva, his divine weapons failed him and many women were carried off.
Arjuna settled the survivors in several places and installed Krishna's great-grandson Vajra as ruler at Indraprastha; some of Krishna's wives entered the fire and others withdrew to the forest.

Yadava destruction was the immediate trigger for the Pandavas' renunciation: on Vyasa's advice Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit and the brothers and Draupadi set out for the Himalaya.
